title.en: Moremi's Vow at the Stream Esinmirin
title.zh: 莫雷米在埃辛米林溪畔的誓願

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the stream Esinmirin where Moremi vowed)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（許願之溪埃辛米林）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I, 'The Legend of Moremi and her Son'

summary.en: Moremi, wife of one of the ancient heroes of Ile-Ife — probably Oranmiyan — was a woman of great beauty and virtue with an only son, Ela or Olurogbo. The Ifes attributed their repeated sufferings under Igbo raids to the displeasure of their gods, for the attackers seemed not to be human beings but gods or demi-gods. Moremi resolved to find out what the Igbos really were: she repaired to the stream Esinmirin and vowed to its deity that if her plans proved successful she would offer the most costly sacrifice she could afford. "But," she said, "if I perish, I perish." She let herself be captured, was given among the booty to the King of the Igbos, learnt all their secrets — the raiders were mere men covered head to foot in Ekan grass and bamboo fibres — and extracted the secret of attacking them: "If your people know how to make a torch, and have the courage to rush amongst them with lighted torches, they cannot stand that."
summary.zh: 莫雷米乃伊費古英雄（或即奧蘭米揚）之妻，貌美德厚，獨子名埃拉（或奧盧羅格博）。伊費人飽受伊格博人劫掠，以為來犯者非人乃神，遂求諸神而無應。莫雷米決意查明真相：她到埃辛米林溪畔向溪神許願，若計成必獻上最貴重的祭品。「但若我死，便死吧。」她故意被擄，作為戰利品之一被獻給伊格博王，贏得信任，探得全部機密——所謂神兵不過是裹著埃坎草與竹纖維的凡人；又從丈夫口中套得破敵之法：「只要你們會造火把，敢舉著火把衝進他們陣中，他們必潰。」

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the fullest written version of the Moremi legend, which Johnson compares to Jephthah's vow and to the Virgin-and-Child story 'perverted'. Moremi remains a honoured heroine of Ife (Edi festival). Cross-ref: yoruba-moremi-igbo-raid (Ogumefu's folk version).

passages.text: Moremi was the wife of one of the ancient heroes of Ile Ife, probably Oranmiyan. She was a woman of great beauty and virtue, and had an only son named Ela or Olurogbo. It happened that the city of Ife was at one time in a state of frequent commotion and unrest, owing to the repeated raids of a tribe of people called the Igbos. The Ifes attributed this affliction and distress to the displeasure of their gods, because those that attacked them from the Igbo territory appeared not to be human beings, but gods or demi-gods, and consequently the Ifes felt they could not withstand them; so these raiders used to make away with easy plunder, including their valuables, with their women and children. For this they propitiated and called upon their gods for help, but received no response.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now this Moremi, fired with zeal and patriotism, was determined to do what she could to free her country from this calamity. She was resolved to find out what these Igbos really were, and how to fight them. To this end she repaired to a stream called Esinmirin, and there made a vow to the deity thereof that if she was enabled to carry out her plans and they proved successful, she would offer to the god the most costly sacrifice she could afford. Her plan was to expose herself to the raiders and get caught, and be taken to their country where she could best learn their secrets. "But," she said, "if I perish, I perish."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the time of the next raid she was caught by the Igbos and taken to their country; being a woman of great beauty, she was given up, amongst others and sundry booty, to their king. Her beauty and virtue soon won her a place in the country and the confidence of the people; she became familiar with all their customs and learnt all their secrets: then she also learnt that those who were such objects of terror to her people were mere men, who covered themselves from head to foot with Ekan grass and bamboo fibres, making them appear extra human, and are nicknamed Eluyare. She extracted from her husband also the secret of attacking them successfully: "If your people know how to make a torch, and have the courage to rush amongst them with lighted torches, they cannot stand that."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Olurogbo, Half Dead on the Altar, Climbs to Heaven
title.zh: 祭壇上半死的奧盧羅格博攀天而去

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the altar where the vow was paid)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（還願的祭壇）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I, 'The Legend of Moremi and her Son'

summary.en: Having freed her country for ever from the raids of the men once their terror, Moremi repaired to the stream with her offerings of lambs, rams and goats; but the god would not accept any of them. She offered a bullock, and the god refused that also. She prayed the priests to divine what would be acceptable, and the god demanded of her her only son. She gave up her only son in sacrifice to the gods in fulfilment of her vows; the Ife nation bewailed her loss and promised to be to her sons and daughters for the loss she had sustained for the salvation of her country. But Olurogbo, when supposed to be killed, was but half dead; he afterwards revived and rose again, and made a rope with which he climbed up into heaven — and all Ifes to this day have a full hope that he will come again to this world and reap the full reward of his good deeds.
summary.zh: 莫雷米以火攻秘計永絕大患之後，攜羊羔、公羊、山羊赴溪還願；神皆不納。獻上公牛，仍遭拒絕。她請祭司占問何物可納，神竟索其獨子。她依誓將獨子獻為祭品；伊費舉國哀慟，許諾永為其兒女，以補她為救國所失。然而祭壇上的奧盧羅格博僅是半死；他甦醒起身，編繩攀天而去——至今伊費人仍深信他終將重返人間，收穫善行的全數報償。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the vow's price and the promised return — a Yoruba death-and-return figure (Johnson notes the confused echo of Jephthah). Strong member of the resurrection cluster. Cross-refs: yoruba-moremi-esinmirin-vow, christian-passion-resurrection.

passages.text: Moremi feeling she was now conversant with everything amongst the Igbos, having disarmed any suspicion they may have entertained of her as a captive, suddenly escaped one day to her native land, and by making use of the secrets she had learnt, freed her country for ever from the raids of the men once their terror. It remained now for her to fulfil her vows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: She repaired to the stream with her offerings of lambs, rams, and goats for sacrifice, but the god would not accept any of these. She then offered a bullock, which the god also refused to accept; then she prayed the priests to divine for her what would be acceptable; this was done, and the god demanded of her her only son! She then gave up her only son in sacrifice to the gods in the fulfilment of her vows. The Ife nation bewailed her loss and promised to be to her sons and daughters, for the loss she had sustained for the salvation of her country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Olurogbo however, when supposed to be killed, was but half dead; he afterwards revived and rose again, and made a rope with which he climbed up into heaven; and all Ifes to this day have a full hope that he will come again to this world, and reap the full reward of his good deeds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Sango Learns His Dead Mother's Name: Torosi
title.zh: 尚戈得知亡母之名——托羅西

region.en: Tapa (Nupe) country (symbolic pin: Elempe's grave where the name was spoken)
region.zh: 塔帕（努佩）之地（象徵定位：埃倫佩王陵——報名之處）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: Sango, possessed with a desire to worship at the grave of his dead mother, could not so much as remember her name — she died when he was but a babe, a daughter of Elempe, the Nupe king who gave her to Oranyan in marriage. He commissioned a Tetu and a Hausa slave to go to the Tapa country and obtain from Elempe a horse and a cow for the sacrifice, charging them to listen carefully to the first name uttered in the invocation, which would be his mother's. The messengers were heartily welcomed and highly entertained; the Hausa forgot himself and his duty, but at the sacrifice the priest said at the grave: "Torosi, iya gbodo, listen to us, thy son Sango is come to worship thee." The Tetu noted the name Torosi; the drunken Hausa paid no heed. On their return the faithful Tetu was highly rewarded and the Hausa slave severely punished — 122 razor cuts slashed all over his body as a lasting warning.
summary.zh: 尚戈欲往亡母陵前致祭，卻連母親的名字也不記得——她在他還是嬰孩時便已去世；她是努佩王埃倫佩嫁給奧蘭揚的女兒。尚戈派一名特圖人與一名豪薩奴隸前往塔帕之地，向埃倫佩求一馬一牛為祭，並囑二人：祭祀時神職呼喊的第一個名字，必是他母親之名。二使受到盛情款待；豪薩人樂而忘形。祭司在墓前祝曰：「托羅西，伊亞格博多，聽著，你的兒子尚戈前來祭拜你了。」特圖人默記「托羅西」；醉醺醺的豪薩人卻渾然不覺。歸國之後，忠謹的特圖人重賞，豪薩奴隸重罰——全身剃刀紋一百二十二道，永為鑒戒。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the Torosi-name and razor-cut etiology in Johnson's royal history — the fuller court version of Ogumefu's tribal-marks tale (yoruba-sango-tribal-marks).

passages.text: Sango was now possessed with a desire of performing an act of filial piety. He wished to worship at the grave of his dead mother, but he did not so much as remember her name, for she died when he was but a babe. She was the daughter of Elempe, a Nupe king, who formed an alliance with Oranyan by giving him his daughter to wife, of which marriage Sango was the issue. Sango therefore commissioned a Tetu and a Hausa slave to proceed to the Tapa country, to his maternal grandfather Elempe, for the purpose of giving them a horse and a cow for the sacrifice. The King's charge to these messengers was, that they should listen carefully to the first name uttered in the invocation which evidently will be his mother's name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The messengers were heartily welcomed and highly entertained by Elempe, their King's grandfather, so much so that the Hausa forgot himself and the duty he was charged with. At the time of the sacrifice, the priest said at the grave: "Torosi, iya gbodo, listen to us, thy son Sango is come to worship thee." The Tetu noted the name Torosi, but the Hausa, being far from sober, paid no heed to what was said; therefore, on their return home, the Tetu who had faithfully carried out his orders was highly rewarded, and the Hausa slave severely punished. The punishment meted out to him was 122 razor cuts slashed all over his body as a lasting warning for all time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Scars That Took the Fancy of the King's Wives
title.zh: 王妃豔羨的疤紋與中計的奧約科羅

region.en: Oyokoro (Oyo), Nigeria (the city whose chiefs were marked as a trap)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約科羅（酋長們受紋中計之城）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: The scars left by the 122 razor cuts strangely took the fancy of the King's wives, who thought they added comeliness and beauty, and advised that such marks should in future be made not upon a slave but on actual members of the royal family as distinctive of royalty. Sango took the advice and placed himself first in the hands of the markers, Babajegbe Osan and Babajegbe Oru; but he could stand only two cuts on each arm — these are the Ey o, two broad ribbon-marks from shoulder to wrist still worn by the royal family, whose members are termed Akeyo. When Sango determined to take Oyokoro, he sent the marked Hausa slave to show how beautiful the marks looked, and advised the prince of Oyokoro to submit himself and his principal chiefs to be thus marked for rank and beauty. On the third day, when they were very sore, Sango appeared with his forces: no resistance could be offered, and the city fell — shamefully and brutally he put to death the prince and his chiefs, the dupes of his stratagem. Thus the seat of government was permanently removed to Oyo.
summary.zh: 那一百二十二道剃刀疤竟令王妃們傾心，以為平添俊美；她們進言：此後刀紋不當施於奴隸，而應行於王室成員之身，以為王族之標記。尚戈率先受紋——由紋師巴巴傑格貝-奧桑與巴巴傑格貝-奧魯執刀——但他只能忍受每臂兩道：這便是「埃約」——肩至腕的兩道寬帶紋，至今仍是王族記號，族人稱「阿凱約」。尚戈欲取奧約科羅，便派帶紋的豪薩奴隸前往示美，勸該城王子與諸酋長為榮銜美觀而受紋。第三日，他們創痛難當之際，尚戈大軍壓境；城中無力抵抗，城池陷落——他殘忍處死中了圈套的王子與酋長們。王都自此永久遷於奧約。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the Akeyo royal marks etiology joined to a stratagem of war, in Johnson's royal history. Executions reported without graphic detail.

passages.text: The scars left by these wounds strangely took the fancy of the King's wives who thought that they added comeliness and beauty to the man, and therefore they advised that in future such marks should not be performed upon a slave, but on actual members of the royal family as distinctive of royalty. Sango took this advice, and placed himself first in the hands of the Olowolas (the markers) named Babajegbe Osan and Babajegbe Oru; but he could stand only two cuts on each arm, and forbade them to proceed any further. This is what is termed Ey o. The marks are to this day retained in the royal family, as a distinctive badge of royalty, and hence members of the royal family are termed Akeyo. They are two broad ribbon marks on the arms from the shoulder to the wrist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the King had determined upon taking Oyokoro, it occurred to him to employ this as a device by which he could effect his purpose easily without loss of lives. He thereupon sent the Hausa slave to Oloyo-koro, for him to see how beautiful this slave looks with these marks, and that it has been resolved to use the same as a mark of royalty; he therefore advised the Oloyo-koro to submit himself to be thus marked, with his principal chiefs for rank and beauty, stating that he himself had done so. To this they consented, and Babajegbe Osan and Babajegbe Oru were sent over there, and admirably did they perform their tasks. But on the third day, when the Oloyo-koro and his chiefs were very sore, Sango appeared with his forces against them; no resistance could be offered, and the city fell easily into his hands: shamefully and brutally he put to death the prince and his chiefs, the dupes of his stratagem. Thus the seat of government was permanently removed from Oko to Oyo the ancient Eyeo or Katunga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Charm Tested on His Own Palace: Sango's Long Road to Koso
title.zh: 咒藥先試己宮——尚戈走向庫索的不歸路

region.en: Oyo and Koso, Nigeria (the hill Oke-Ajaka above the burning palace)
region.zh: 奧約與庫索（焚宮所在的奧凱-阿賈卡山）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: Sango reigned seven years, marked by restlessness; he was said to have the knowledge of a preparation by which he could attract lightning. The palace at Oyo stood at the foot of the hill Oke-Ajaka; one day the King ascended it with his courtiers and slaves, among them his two favourites Biri and Omiran, minded to try the preparation — thinking it might have been damp and useless, he first made the experiment on his own house. A storm was raised, the lightning struck the palace before they came down the hill, and the buildings were on fire; many of Sango's wives and children perished. From a broken heart he resolved to abdicate and retire to the court of his maternal grandfather Elempe; all Oyo was astir to dissuade him, but he could not bear opposition and slew with his own sword some of the loyal subjects who remonstrated; he was said to have caused 160 persons to be slain in a fit of anger. Setting out with a few followers, his favourites Biri and Omiran one after another regretted the step and forsook him; left alone, ashamed to return, he climbed a shea-butter tree and hanged himself.
summary.zh: 尚戈在位七年，征伐不休；相傳他通曉一種引雷之法。奧約王宮築於奧凱-阿賈卡山麓；一日王與近臣、奴僕（含寵臣比里與奧米蘭）登山，欲試其藥——只因疑心藥已受潮失效，竟先在自己宮殿上試驗。頃刻風暴大作，眾人尚未下山，雷已殛宮，烈焰沖天；尚戈的多位妻室與子孫葬身火中。他心碎欲狂，決意退位投奔外祖埃倫佩。全城苦諫，他卻容不得半點異議，親手斬殺進言的忠臣；一怒之下被殺者達一百六十人。他僅攜少數隨從啟程；寵臣比里、奧米蘭先後悔悟棄他而去。孤身無助、歸又無顏，他攀上一株乳油木，自縊於枝頭。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; Johnson's full court version of the charm-fire and flight (complementing Ogumefu yoruba-sango-lightning-storm and Frobenius's variants). Suicide reported as the recorded tradition states it.

passages.text: Sango reigned for seven years, the whole of which period was marked by his restlessness. He fought many battles and was fond of making charms. He was said to have the knowledge of some preparation by which he could attract lightning. The palace at Oyo was built at the foot of a hill called Oke Ajaka (Ajaka's hill). One day the King ascended this hill accompanied by his courtiers and some of his slaves, among whom were two favourites, Biri and Omiran; some of his cousins went with him, but none of his children. He was minded to try the preparation he had in hand; thinking it might have been damp and useless, he first made the experiment on his own house. But it took effect: a storm was immediately raised and the lightning had struck the palace before they came down the hill, and the buildings were on fire. Many of Sango's wives and his children perished in this catastrophe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sango, who was the author of his own misfortunes, became alarmed and dismayed at what had happened, and from a broken heart he was resolved to abdicate the throne and retire to the court of his maternal grandfather, Elempe, king of the Nupes. All Oyo was now astir, not only to sympathize with the King, but also to dissuade him from carrying out his resolution; but he could not bear any opposition, and so mad was he that he even used his sword against some of his loyal subjects who ventured to remonstrate with him, and who promised to replace for him his dead wives by others. He was said to have caused 160 persons to be slain in a fit of anger, of those who were showing much concern and over-anxiety on his behalf, and who would prevent him by force from carrying out his resolve.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thus determined he set out on his fateful journey with a few followers. Biri his head slave and favourite was the first to regret the step taken, and to urge on his master to yield to the entreaties of those citizens of Oyo who with all loyalty promised to replace his losses and rebuild the palace; but finding the King inexorable, he forsook him and returned to the city with all his followers; Omiran likewise followed his example, and the King was thus left alone. He now repented his rashness, especially when he found himself deserted by his favourite Biri. He could not proceed alone, and for shame he could not return home, and so he was resolved to put an end to his own life; and climbing on a shea butter tree, he hanged himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: They Died With Their King: Biri at Koso, Oya at Ira
title.zh: 以身殉王——比里歿於庫索，奧雅歿於伊拉

region.en: Koso, Ira, Papo, Sele and Jakuta, near Oyo, Nigeria (the suicide-sites of the King's party)
region.zh: 庫索、伊拉、帕波、塞萊與賈庫塔（近奧約，王黨殉節之地）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: On hearing of the King's death his personal friends followed his example and died with him: Biri committed suicide at Koso (where the King died), Omiran did the same, his cousin Omo Sinda at Papo, Babayanmi at Sele, Obei at Jakuta, and Oya his favourite wife at Ira. Sango was afterwards deified and is still worshipped by all of the Yoruba race as the god of thunder and lightning; in every Yoruba and Popo town, whenever a flash of lightning is followed by a peal of thunder, the populace shouts "Ka biye si" — welcome to your majesty, long live the King. Deified heroes and heroines are never spoken of as dead, but as having disappeared: "Oya disappeared in the town of Ira; Sango disappeared at Koso."
summary.zh: 噩耗傳來，王的近臣相繼以身相殉：比里歿於庫索（王崩之地），奧米蘭同之，堂親奧莫辛達歿於帕波，巴巴揚米歿於塞萊，奧貝歿於賈庫塔，愛妃奧雅歿於伊拉。尚戈後被尊為神，至今全約魯巴人奉為雷電之神；凡約魯巴與波波城鎮，電光之後雷聲一響，民眾便高呼「卡比耶西」——恭迎王駕，國王萬歲！成神者從不言「死」，只道「隱去」：諺云「奧雅隱於伊拉城，尚戈隱於庫索山」。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the martyr-list and disappearance formula. Suicides within the recorded tradition; reported without graphic detail.

passages.text: His friends hearing of this tragedy went immediately and performed for him the last act of kindness, by burying his remains under the same tree. On hearing of the King's death, his personal friends followed his example, and died with him: Biri committed suicide at Koso (where the King died), Omiran did the same, his cousin Omo Sinda committed suicide at Papo, Babayanmi at Sele, Obei at Jakuta, and Oya his favourite wife at Ira.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thus ended the life of this remarkable personage, who once ruled over all the Yorubas and Popos. He was afterwards deified, and is still worshipped by all of the Yoruba race as the god of thunder and lightning. In every Yoruba and Popo town to this day, whenever there is a flash of lightning followed by a peal of thunder, it is usual to hear from the populace shouts of "Ka biye si" (welcome to your majesty, long live the King). Deified heroes and heroines are never spoken of as dead, but as having disappeared. Thus the saying: "Oya wole ni ile Ira, Sango wole ni Koso" — Oya disappeared in the town of Ira, Sango disappeared at Koso.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Ajaka and the Nine Medicine-Men Who Could Not Be Kept
title.zh: 阿賈卡與留不住的九位術士

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the royal court where the magicians vanished)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（術士遁走的宮廷）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: King Ajaka kept in his service medicine-men who made charms for him — Atagbin, Omo-onikoko, Abitibiti Onisegun, Paku, Teteoniru, Yonk, Oko-adan Egbeji, Alari baba isegun, and Elenre. After his wars, some humbly prayed to be allowed to return home; the King refused, fearing lest other kings might come into possession of the charms they had made. As they were determined to go, they showed by demonstrative proofs that the request was but courtesy: Paku fell down before him and disappeared; Teteoniru, Abitibiti Onisegun and Alari did the same; Egbeji threw up a ball of thread which hung suspended in space, climbed it and vanished. Elenre alone remained standing. "Kill me if you can," he replied; the sword broke in two, the spear bent and the spearman's arm withered, the great stone fell on him as light as a ball of cotton-wool.
summary.zh: 阿賈卡王豢養九位術士為他造符：阿塔格賓、奧莫-奧尼科科、阿比提比提、帕庫、泰特奧尼魯、約恩克、奧科-阿丹埃格貝吉、阿拉里與埃倫雷。戰事既畢，諸術士謙辭還鄉；王恐符咒落入他國之手而不許。他們遂以實證表明去意難留：帕庫當場倒地隱沒；泰特奧尼魯、阿比提比提、阿拉里相繼消失；埃格貝吉拋出一團懸空的線球，攀線升空而去。唯埃倫雷屹立不動。「殺我？你若能！」寶劍應聲兩斷，長矛彎折、矛手手臂枯萎，巨石壓身輕如棉絮。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; Johnson's royal version of the magicians' contest (cf. Ogumefu yoruba-three-magicians-elenre), with Johnson's own note that the fable is Elijah 'in a perverted form'.

passages.text: He had in his service certain medicine men who made charms for him, viz., Atagbin, Omo-onikoko, Abitibiti Onisegun, Paku, Teteoniru, Yonk, Oko-adan Egbeji, Alari baba isegun, and Elenre. After his wars, some of these medicine men went up to him and humbly prayed to be allowed to return home; but the King refused to grant them leave, fearing lest their services might be required by some other kings, and in that way others might be in possession of the charms they made for him. As they were determined to go home they showed the King by demonstrative proofs that they made the request simply out of courtesy but that the King could not detain them: Paku fell down before him, and disappeared. Teteoniru, Abitibiti Onisegun, and Alari baba Isegun performed the same feat and vanished. Egbeji threw up a ball of thread which hung suspended in space, and he climbed up it and disappeared. Elenre alone remained standing before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then said the King to him: "Elenre, you had better follow the examples of your colleagues and vanish, or I shall wreak my vengeance upon you for their disobedience." "Kill me if you can," replied Elenre. The King thereupon ordered him to be decapitated; but the sword was broken in two on the attempt. He then ordered him to be speared, but the spear became bent and the spearman's arm withered! He ordered a large stone to be rolled over him to crush him to death, but it fell on him as light as a ball of cotton-wool.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Head in the King's Hand Becomes a River
title.zh: 王掌中的頭顱化作長河

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (Odo Elenre, Elenre's river, and Ijaechin's stagnant pool)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（埃倫雷之河與伊亞埃欽的死水潭）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: The King and executioners were at their wits' end until one bethought himself to "plough with his heifer": Elenre's wife Ijaechin, prevailed upon, told them that no iron or steel could affect him — "Pull off a single blade of grass from the thatch of the house, and with that you can decapitate him." This was done; but instead of falling to the ground the head fell into the King's hand, and he involuntarily grasped it. He tried all he could to drop it, to no avail: any food brought to the King the head devoured, and drank all the water likewise, and the King, famishing, was really dying of hunger. Medicine-men of every tribe were sent for; as soon as anyone entered, the head would call him by name, tell out the composition of his charms, and ask "Do you think that can affect me?" — until came Agawo, who prostrated at a distance and entreated: "Who am I to oppose you? I came only in obedience to the King's commands, as I dare not refuse to come." "I will respect you because you are wise and respect yourself; I yield to your entreaties." Then, falling suddenly from the King's hands, Elenre's head became a flowing river known at Oyo to this day as Odo Elenre. His wife Ijaechin, who disclosed the secret, was also converted into a stream — but Elenre's head said to it "Thou shalt not flow," and she became a stagnant pool. From this incident King Ajaka made it a rule that no king should be present in person at an execution.
summary.zh: 君臣束手無策之際，有人想起「借他家中母牛犁田」：埃倫雷之妻伊亞埃欽受迫吐露——鋼鐵傷他不得，「從屋頂茅草抽一根草葉，便能斷他首級」。依計行之，頭顱落地卻不墜地，竟落進王掌之中，王身不由己緊握不放。任何飲食送到王前，那頭顱便吃盡喝光；王餓得形容枯槁，幾乎喪命。全國術士奉召前來驅邪——誰一進門，頭顱便喚其名、報出其符方，問「你以為這能奈何我？」直至阿加奧前來，遠遠俯伏哀求：「我何德何能敢與您為敵？我不過奉王命而來，不敢不來。」頭顱答：「你自重，我亦敬你；我依你所請。」言畢頭顱驟然離手落地，化作奔流長河——即今日奧約的「埃倫雷之河」。洩密的伊亞埃欽也化為溪流，頭顱卻道「你不許流動」，遂成死水一潭。自此阿賈卡王定規：君王永不親臨刑場。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the river-and-pool etiology completing the Elenre cycle (Johnson notes the Jordan parallel in his Elijah comparison). Cross-ref: yoruba-three-magicians-elenre.

passages.text: The King and the executioners were now at their wits' end, and then it occurred to one of them to plough with his heifer. His wife Ijaechin being prevailed upon, told them that no iron or steel can affect him: "Pull off a single blade of grass from the thatch of the house, and with that you can decapitate him." This was done, and the head was struck off, but instead of falling to the ground, it fell into the King's hand, and he involuntarily grasped it. The King tried all his best to drop it off, but to no avail. Any food brought to the King the head devoured, and drank all the water likewise. The King soon became famished, he was losing flesh, and was really dying from hunger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: All the medicine men of every tribe in the kingdom were sent for, to disenchant this alarming phenomenon: as soon as anyone entered, the head would call him by name, tell out the composition of his charms, and then ask "Do you think that can affect me?" Thus many were baffled, until at last came one Agawo; this man at once prostrated at a distance and entreated the head to forbear with him, saying: "Who am I to oppose you? In what am I better than my predecessors whom you have already foiled? I came only in obedience to the King's commands as I dare not refuse to come." The head replied: "I will respect you because you are wise and respect yourself; I yield to your entreaties." Then, falling suddenly from the King's hands, Elenre's head became a flowing river known at Oyo to this day as Odo Elenre (Elenre's river). His wife Ijaechin who disclosed the secret of his strength was also converted into a stream, but Elenre's head said to it "Thou shalt not flow," therefore Ijaechin became a stagnant pool at Oyo unto this day. From this incident King Ajaka made it a rule that from henceforth no King should be present in person at an execution.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Ajaka's Birds of War Across the Niger
title.zh: 阿賈卡的飛鳥大軍渡尼日河

region.en: The Niger crossing, Tapa country (symbolic pin: the Niger where the birds flew)
region.zh: 塔帕之地的尼日渡口（象徵定位：飛鳥掠過的尼日河）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: King Ajaka, dethroned for being too peaceful, proved after his re-instatement a totally different man, more warlike even than his brother Sango. He led an expedition into the Tapa country, and tradition has it that he employed large and well-trained birds armed with arrows, and after crossing the Niger they showered down these deadly weapons upon the maternal relations of his brother Sango. What is certain is that the expedition was successful — but by what means it is not really known; for with the Yorubas, as with all superstitious peoples, brave deeds and extraordinary acts of daring are always attributed to the supernatural.
summary.zh: 因太過溫和而一度被廢的阿賈卡王，復位後判若兩人，比其兄尚戈更好征戰。他領兵遠征塔帕之地；相傳他動用受過大規模訓練的飛鳥，鳥爪縛箭，渡過尼日河後，便向其兄尚戈的母系親族漫天傾瀉這些奪命之矢。可以確定的是征伐大獲全勝——至於用何手段，實難考證；因為約魯巴人一如所有崇信神異的民族，凡勇武奇功，皆歸於超自然之力。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; a marvel-tale of archer-birds reported by Johnson with his own sceptical note.

passages.text: King Ajaka who was dethroned for being too peaceful was now recalled to the throne. He proved after his re-instatement a totally different man to what he had been before, and showed himself more warlike than even his brother Sango. He led an expedition into the Tapa country. Tradition has it that he employed large and well-trained birds, armed with arrows, and after crossing the Niger they showered down these deadly weapons upon the maternal relations of his brother Sango. What is certain is that the expedition was successful, but by what means it is not really known. But thus it was with the Yorubas, as with all superstitious people, that brave deeds and extraordinary acts of daring are always attributed to the supernatural.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Thousand Skulls Worshipped as Orishala
title.zh: 千顆骷髏——奧里夏拉崇拜之源

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the reliquary of skulls kept in the royal city)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（王城中的骷髏聖龕）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. I

summary.en: Ajaka spent the latter part of his years waging intestine wars with 1060 of his chiefs and princes, among them the principal vassal kings, the Onikoyi, the Olugbon and the Aresa. He put to death all the vassal kings, 1060 in number, taken in war; the relics of their skulls were put together and are worshipped under the name of Orishala to this day — this, says Johnson, is the probable origin of that worship. He goes on to read the reign of the mythological heroes as garbled forms of scriptural stories: Elijah's slaughter of the priests of Baal perverted into Ajaka slaying his vassal kings, Egbeji climbing a cord into heaven as Elijah's ascent, Elenre's head becoming a river as Jordan was crossed.
summary.zh: 阿賈卡晚年與一千零六十名酋長王子連年內戰——其中不乏奧尼科伊、奧盧貢、阿雷薩等大藩之王。他把戰敗被俘的一千零六十位藩王盡數處死；其頭骨遺骸收集一處，至今以「奧里夏拉」之名受人崇拜——約翰遜認為，這很可能就是該崇拜的源頭。他又指出，這些神話時代君王的傳說皆是聖經故事的訛變：以利亞屠殺巴力眾祭司，被改寫成阿賈卡誅殺千位藩王；埃格貝吉攀繩上天，猶如以利亞升天；埃倫雷頭顱化河，彷彿約旦河的渡越。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; cult-origin legend with mass execution of vassal kings reported as the recorded tradition states it, non-graphically. Johnson's Biblical-parallelistic reading is his own and is reported as such.

passages.text: He spent the latter part of his years in waging intestine wars with his subjects. He was said to have been engaged in civil wars with 1060 of his chiefs and princes, among whom were the principal vassal or provincial kings, the Onikoyi, the Olugbon, and the Aresa. He put to death all the vassal kings, 1060 in number, taken in war; the relics of their skulls were put together and are worshipped under the name of Orishala to this day. This is the probable origin of that worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The reign of the mythological heroes abound in garbled forms of scriptural stories, showing, as was remarked in the earlier part of this history, that the ancestors of the Yorubas were acquainted with Christianity in the land of their origin. The fable here related is evidently the story of Elijah in a perverted form: his putting to death so many priests of Baal has been perverted into Ajaka slaying all his vassal kings and their skulls converted to an object of worship; Egbeji climbing up a cord and disappearing as the saying goes, Egbeji ta kun o lo si Orun — Egbeji suspended a cord and by it went up to heaven; and the river Jordan crossed by Elijah suggested Elenre's head becoming a river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Gbonka Sits in the Fire and Walks Out of It

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the single combat and the pyre in the royal court)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（宮廷決鬥與柴堆）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. II

summary.en: Timi, the kinglet of Ede who had stopped paying his tribute of five cowries per trader, routed the King's troops. Eliri-onigbajo the Gbonka — the only man who dared oppose the King's own encroachments — was appointed to bring him in, the King secretly hoping his champion might fall. In the single combat Gbonka carried a viol of a drug with strong narcotic properties when inhaled, and Timi, rendered unconscious, was dispossessed and taken bound to Oyo. The King, pretending to doubt the fairness of the fight, ordered it repeated before him; Gbonka was again victorious, and Timi was instantaneously killed by the victor before the King and without his orders. To strike terror into the King, Gbonka ordered a pile made and pots of palm oil, nut oil and shea butter poured on it, went coolly and sat on the top, and ordered it set on fire — and when the pile was ablaze, the Gbonka disappeared. Tidings soon reached the court that he was seen dancing about the town; he entered the palace and challenged His Majesty to display feats similar to his own — and the King, having no alternative, took poison and died.
summary.zh: 伊德的小王蒂米停繳每商五貝幣的稅金，還擊潰了王師。宮中舉薦貢邦卡（埃利里-奧尼加喬）——唯一敢於抗衡王權擴張之人——前去拿人；王暗自指望他的勇士命喪其手。單打獨鬥中，貢邦卡攜一只嗅之即昏迷的藥瓶，蒂米不省人事，被繳械縛送奧約。王假意懷疑勝負是否公平，命二人當廷再戰；貢邦卡再勝，竟未奉王命當場擊斃蒂米。為震懾君王，貢邦卡命人堆起柴垛，澆以棕櫚油、堅果油與乳油，自己泰然坐上柴頂，命人點火——烈焰騰起，貢邦卡蹤影全無。不久王廷傳來消息：他正隨鼓手在城中起舞！他闖進王宮，喝令君王也顯一手同樣的神通——國王別無他法，服毒自盡。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the fire-ordeal of Gbonka mirrors Shango's fire-pile motif (cf. yoruba-shango-fire-pile-resurrection) in a court-legend register. Executions reported without graphic detail.

passages.text: Eliri-onigbajo the Gbonka was proposed to the King as the only man equal to the task of arresting Timi. But the Gbonka was already a powerful subject at Oyo, being the only man who dared to oppose the King's encroachments upon the liberties of the people; therefore he was at first loth to accede to this proposal, lest a success might add an additional lustre to the Gbonka's glory; but on second consideration he consented, secretly hoping he might fall by the hand of his brave antagonist. So the Gbonka was appointed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fight was limited to a single combat between the two chieftains. Timi armed himself with his bow and arrows, but the Gbonka carried a shield with which to defend himself against the powerful darts of his assailant. His own weapon of offence was a viol containing a drug with strong narcotic properties when inhaled, and by means of this Timi was soon rendered unconscious, and in this state he was dispossessed of his weapons and taken bound to Oyo. The King, pretending to be dissatisfied with the issue of the contest, doubting its fairness, ordered the same to be repeated in his presence. To his mortification the Gbonka was again victorious amid shouts of applause from the people. Timi was not only subdued but was also instantaneously killed by the victor before the King and without his orders.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Gbonka, to show further what he could do, and to strike terror into the King, ordered a pile to be made, and pots of palm oil, nut oil, and shea butter to be poured on it; he then went coolly and sat on the top of it, and ordered it to be set on fire. All present were anxious for the consequence; but when the pile was ablaze, the Gbonka disappeared. Courtiers now began to congratulate the King on the fall of his enemy by his own hands; but he was apprehensive of some other issues. Tidings soon reached the court that the Gbonka, followed by drummers, was seen dancing about the town. The Gbonka, knowing the public feeling towards the King and his unpopularity, entered the palace and challenged His Majesty to display feats similar to his own, and said if he could not, he would be rejected. There being no alternative, the King took poison and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Oluaso: The King of 320 Years and Three Sets of Twins
title.zh: 奧盧阿索——在位三百二十年與三對雙生

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the fifty-four palaces of the royal twins)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（五十四座王宮）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. II

summary.en: The unfortunate King was succeeded by a handsome and amiable prince called Oluaso, remarkable for his longevity and peaceful reign — his agnomen Osarewa S'akin, handsome but strong. He was a wise and affable sovereign fabled to have reigned 320 years and had 1460 children! Three times did nine of his wives bear him male twins in one day: the first set he named Omoja, the second Ona-aka, and the third Ona-isokun. Of these three sets of twins the last were the most popular, and kings were chosen from amongst them and their descendants; these names have become hereditary titles unto this day. The King built fifty-four palaces for them.
summary.zh: 不幸的國王之後，繼位的是俊美和藹的王子奧盧阿索，以長壽與太平之治著稱——綽號「奧薩雷瓦薩金」，俊美而剛強。相傳這位賢君在位三百二十年，得子女一千四百六十人！一日之間，九位王妃竟三度為他誕下男嬰雙生：第一對名奧莫賈，第二對奧納阿卡，第三對奧納伊索昆。三對之中，末對最得人望，歷代君王皆出自這一系及其後裔；這些名字至今仍為世襲尊號。國王為他們建了五十四座宮殿。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the hyperbolic reign-lengths and triple twin-births of Oluaso, anchoring the Ona-isokun royal line. Cross-refs: yoruba-ondo-twins-exile, yoruba-ibeji-ere-figures.

passages.text: The unfortunate King was succeeded by a handsome and amiable prince called Oluaso, who was remarkable for his longevity and peaceful reign. His agnomen was Osarewa S'akin, i.e., handsome but strong. He was a wise and affable sovereign fabled to have reigned for 320 years, and had 1460 children! Three times did nine of his wives bear him male twins in one day. The first set he named Omoja, the second Ona-aka, and the third Ona-isokun. Of these three sets of twins the last (Ona-isokun) were the most popular, and kings were chosen from amongst them and their descendants. These names have become hereditary titles unto this day. The King built 54 palaces for these.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Son Prayed For at the Grave: Iyayun and Kori
title.zh: 陵前求來的兒子——伊亞貴與科里

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (Aganju's grave where the dynasty's survival was prayed for)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（在阿甘朱陵前求嗣之地）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part II ch. II

summary.en: Aganju, Ajaka's son who tamed wild animals and venomous reptiles and kept a tame leopard, waged war at the end of his reign on a namesake, the Onisambo, for refusing him the hand of his daughter Iyayun: four chiefs were captured, their towns destroyed, and the bride forcibly secured. His only son Lubego was discovered in illicit intercourse with the beloved Iyayun; the stern father pronounced the extreme penalty, and it was rigidly carried out — but the King was overcome with grief and died soon after, before the birth of a successor. The late king having no surviving son, the Basorun Erankogbina managed the kingdom, and the only hope of a direct successor was the child of Iyayun still unborn: sacrifices were offered frequently on the grave of Aganju, praying him to grant Iyayun a son, if his name was not to be forgotten and the dynasty end with him. When in due course Iyayun gave birth to a son, the joy of the populace was unbounded; he was named Kori. During Kori's minority Iyayun was declared Regent: she wore the crown, put on the royal robes, and was invested with the Ejigba, the Opa ileke and other royal insignia, and ruled the kingdom as a man until her son was of age.
summary.zh: 阿賈卡之子阿甘朱能馴服猛獸毒蛇，還養著一頭溫馴的花豹。他晚年為強娶同名藩王奧尼桑博之女伊亞貴而興兵：四位酋長被擒、城池被毀、新娘被強奪。其獨子盧貝戈竟與愛妃伊亞貴私通；嚴父判以極刑，依法執行——但國王悲慟欲絕，未及見嗣子出生便撒手人寰。先王無嗣，巴西倫埃蘭科格比納代攝國政；王統唯一的希望是伊亞貴腹中的孩子：人們頻頻到阿甘朱陵前獻祭，禱求他賜伊亞貴一子，否則他的名號將被遺忘、王朝亦將終絕。伊亞貴果真誕下男嬰，萬民歡騰；孩子取名科里。科里年幼，伊亞貴被立為攝政：她戴上王冠、穿上王服、受「埃吉巴」權杖與「奧帕伊萊克」等御物，儼然以男子之姿治國，直至兒子成年。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; a queen-regent legend with posthumous-heir grave-prayers. The execution of Lubego is reported without graphic detail.

passages.text: Aganju, Ajaka's son, had a remarkable faculty of taming wild animals and venomous reptiles, several of which may be seen crawling about him; he had also in his house a tame leopard. Towards the end of his reign he waged war with a namesake of his, Aganju the Onisambo, for refusing him the hand of his daughter Iyayun. In this war four chiefs, viz. the Onisambo and his allies the Onitede, the Onimeri and the Alagbona, were captured, their towns destroyed, and the bride forcibly secured. The close of his reign was clouded by great domestic troubles: his only son Lubego was discovered having illicit intercourse with his beloved Iyayun, on whose account so many princes and people have lost their lives. The stern father was enraged beyond words, the sentence pronounced on him was the extreme penalty of the law, and it was rigidly carried out. But the King was overcome with grief; he died not long after this, even before the birth of a successor to the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The late King having no surviving son, Erankogbina the Basorun was left to manage the affairs of the kingdom. The only hope of a direct successor to the throne was the child of Iyayun still in utero; hence sacrifices were offered frequently on the grave of Aganju, praying him to grant Iyayun a son, if his name is not to be forgotten and the dynasty end with him. When in due course therefore Iyayun gave birth to a son, the joy of the populace was unbounded; he was named Kori. During Kori's minority, Iyayun was declared Regent; she wore the crown, and put on the royal robes, and was invested with the Ejigba, the Opa ileke and other royal insignia, and ruled the kingdom as a man until her son was of age.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part II ch. II (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: "My Father Will Find the Koran for Me"

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the Basorun's house struck the next morning)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（次日遭雷擊的巴西倫宅邸）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part III ch. I

summary.en: One Alaja-eta, a Hausa trader at Oyo, was plundered of his goods under the pretext that he was bringing bad charms into the city; among the confiscated goods was his Koran, which he prized more than all else. He appealed to King Aole, who from a sense of justice ordered everything restored — all but the Koran. The Hausa appealed again; the King insisted that search be made and the lost Koran restored. The Basorun, in whose possession it probably was, refused, and told the King it could not be found. His Majesty felt this keenly as an insult to his dignity: "Very well then, if you cannot find it, my father (meaning the deified Sango) will find the Koran for me." As the god Sango is reputed to take vengeance on thieves and liars by burning their houses, so the next day, when lightning struck the Basorun's house, great was his rage against the King for being instrumental in convicting him of theft and lying — the ceremony of appeasing the god entailing heavy expenses on him who, had it been another man's house, might have gone shares in the fines. Thus he became the King's enemy.
summary.zh: 奧約城中的豪薩商人阿拉賈-埃塔被誣「攜邪符入城」，貨物盡遭搶奪；被抄之物中有一部他視若性命的《可蘭經》。他向阿奧萊王申冤；王秉公下令全數發還——唯經書未還。豪薩人再訴，王堅持搜查歸還。經書多半在巴西倫（首相）之手，他卻拒不交出，回稟「查無此物」。國王深以為辱：「好——你既尋不著，我父（即指已故成神的尚戈）自會為我尋回！」尚戈素以火焚宅第懲治竊賊謊者；次日雷電果然擊中巴西倫的房屋。他怒不可遏——王藉神明之力坐實了他竊盜與說謊之罪，而安神謝罪的巨費本可由他分潤罰金。自此他成了國王的死敵。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the lightning-justice episode that opens the Oyo revolution, in Johnson's historical narrative.

passages.text: One Alaja-eta, a Hausa trader at Oyo, was plundered of his goods, under the pretext that he was bringing bad charms into the city. Among his confiscated goods was his Koran, which he prized more than all his other stolen property. He appealed to the King, and he, from a sense of justice, ordered that all his goods be restored to him. All but the Koran were accordingly restored. The Hausa again appealed to the King for this his most valued treasure; the King insisted that search should be made and the lost Koran be restored. The Basorun, in whose possession it probably was, or who at any rate knew where it could be found, refused to restore it, and told the King it could not be found!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: His Majesty felt this keenly as an insult to his dignity; he was heard to say: "Is it come to this that my commands cannot be obeyed in my own capital? Must it be said that I failed to redress the grievance of a stranger in my town? That he appealed to me in vain?" Turning to the Basorun and pointing upwards, he said: "Very well then, if you cannot find it, my father (meaning the deified Sango) will find the Koran for me." As the god Sango is reputed to take vengeance on thieves and liars by burning their houses, so the next day, when lightning struck the Basorun's house, great was his rage against the King for being instrumental in convicting him of theft and lying! The ceremony of appeasing the god by the devotees entailed heavy expenses on the Basorun, who, had it been another man's house, might have gone shares with the Alafin in the fines imposed upon the sufferers. In this way he became the King's enemy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Apata Odaju, the Rock of the Heartless
title.zh: 阿帕塔奧達茹——無情者之岩

region.en: Apomu, Nigeria (the frontier market and the rock where the sold friend was rescued)
region.zh: 奈及利亞阿波穆（邊貿市集與救人時的無情之岩）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part III ch. I

summary.en: Apomu was the market town where Oyos, Ifes, Owus and Ijebus met for trade, in Ife territory on the border of the Olowu's dominion; raiding and man-stealing were rife, and Oyos coming from afar were in the greatest danger. Aole, then a private man, used to trade there with a friend who was also his attendant — and on one occasion he bartered away his own friend for merchandise! The Ijebus were actually taking him away when word reached the Bale of Apomu that an Oyo man was being sold; by the Bale's prompt action the man was rescued at a spot named Apata Odaju, the rock of the heartless. Investigation showed who the slave-dealer was; but as Aole was an Akeyo, a prince, who could not be more severely dealt with, he was ordered by the Bale to be severely flogged — and when Aole came to the throne he named the Bale of Apomu as his enemy, and Apomu was doomed. The faithful Bale took refuge with the Ooni of Ife, his over-lord, but the offence being against the Suzerain, even the Ooni could not save him: to save his town and people from destruction he committed suicide, and his head was cut off and sent to Oyo to appease the offended monarch.
summary.zh: 阿波穆是奧約人、伊費人、奧武人與伊傑布人互市的邊貿重鎮，地處伊費境內、奧洛烏轄區邊緣；掠人販奴之風盛行，遠道而來的奧約人首當其衝。布衣時代的阿奧萊常與一位兼任侍從的好友在此貿易——他竟把摯友折價換了貨物！伊傑布人正要將人帶走時，有人報知阿波穆的巴萊：有奧約人正被販賣。巴萊當機立斷，在一處名叫「阿帕塔奧達茹」——無情者之岩——的地方將人救下。查明販奴者正是阿奧萊；但他是王族「阿凱約」，不能重懲，巴萊便下令重責鞭刑。阿奧萊登基後，點名巴萊為敵，阿波穆遂遭滅頂之災。忠直的巴萊投奔宗主奧尼求庇，但此仇直犯宗主，奧尼亦無能為力；為免全城生靈塗炭，他自盡殉城，頭顱被送往奧約以平息盛怒的君王。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the slave-selling anecdote and the loyal Bale's suicide that sparked the destruction of Apomu. Suicide reported as the recorded tradition states it.

passages.text: Apomu was the market town where Oyos, Ifes, Owus, and Ijebus met for trade. It was situated in Ife territory, and in the border of the Olowu's dominion. Raiding and man-stealing were rife at those times. Oyos particularly were in greater danger, as they came from afar. Aole, who was then a private man, used to trade in these parts with a friend who was also his attendant; and on one occasion, he bartered away his friend for merchandise! So faithless and heartless were the princes in those days. The Ijebus were actually taking him away when it was reported to the Bale of Apomu that an Oyo man was being sold away; fortunately for the man, by the prompt action of the Bale, he was rescued at a certain spot named Apata Odaju (the rock of the heartless), perhaps so named from this circumstance, and brought before the Bale.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Investigation soon showed who the slave-dealer was; but as Aole was an Akeyo (Prince) and could not more severely be dealt with, in order that justice may not miscarry, he was ordered by the Bale to be severely flogged. This was the reason why Aole now named the Bale of Apomu as his enemy, and hence Apomu was doomed. When the Bale of Apomu heard that war was declared against his town on his account, he took refuge in the court of the Ooni of Ife his over-lord, whose orders he had obeyed. But as the offence was against the Suzerain, even the Ooni could not save him; so this faithful chief, in order to save his town and his people from destruction, committed suicide, and his head was cut off and sent to Oyo to appease the offended monarch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Aole's Three Arrows: The Curse That Broke the Empire
title.zh: 阿奧萊的三支箭——裂帝國之咒

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the palace quadrangle where the arrows were loosed)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（放箭發咒的王宮庭院）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part III ch. I

summary.en: Sent against Iwere — impregnable to the simple weapons of the day — under oaths binding the Kakanfo to conquer within three months or die, the army mutinied before its walls: "O Ya!" — now is the time — and the royal party was massacred. Forty-two days the insurgent army stood before Oyo; at last an empty covered calabash was sent to the King — for his head. There being no alternative, His Majesty set his house in order; but before he committed suicide he stepped out into the palace quadrangle with face stern and resolute, carrying in his hands an earthenware dish and three arrows. He shot one to the North, one to the South, and one to the West, uttering those ever-memorable imprecations: "My curse be on ye for your disloyalty and disobedience, so let your children disobey you. If you send them on an errand, let them never return to bring you word again. To all the points I shot my arrows will ye be carried as slaves. My curse will carry you to the sea and beyond the seas; slaves will rule over you, and you their masters will become slaves." Then he raised and dashed the earthenware dish on the ground, smashing it into pieces: "Igba la isu a ki isu awo, beheni ki oru mi o se to! to!" — a broken calabash can be mended, but not a broken dish; so let my words be — irrevocable! He then took poison and died, after which the camp was broken up and each of the chiefs repaired to his own place; from this time the spirit of rebellion spread throughout the kingdom, and tribute was no longer paid to the King.
summary.zh: 卡坎佛（大元帥）受誓約束：三月不克，唯有自裁。諸侯便設計把大軍誘到天險奧維雷城下，軍中一聲「奧雅！」——時機已到——王黨盡遭屠戮。叛軍圍奧約四十二日；末了，一只有蓋空葫蘆被送入宮中——向王索頭。君王自知無路可走，先安排好家事；臨終之前，他面色沉毅地走進王宮庭院，手捧一件陶盤與三支箭。他向北、向南、向西各射一箭，朗聲立下永載史冊的咒誓：「爾等不忠不順，我咒爾等！爾之子孫亦必忤逆爾等。爾差遣他們辦事，叫他們一去不回、音信全無。我箭射向何方，爾等便被賣作奴隸流落何方。我的詛咒要把你們帶到海濱、越過重洋；奴隸將統治你們，而你們這些主人也要淪為奴隸。」隨後他把陶盤高舉擲地，摔得粉碎：「葫蘆碎了尚可修補，陶盤碎了便無可挽回——我言已出，絕不更改！」言畢服毒而崩。叛營隨之散去，諸侯各歸封地；自此叛離之風蔓延全國，貢賦再也不入王庭。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the famous dying curse of Aole (Arogangan), the prophetic charter of the Yoruba nineteenth-century wars and slave-raiding in Johnson's history. Suicide reported as the recorded tradition states it. Cross-tradition cluster: prophetic curse (cf. celtic-fedelm-prophecy-red).

passages.text: The King's counsellors advised that the Kakanfo and the army should be sent against Iwere, a place fortified by nature and by art, and impregnable to the simple weapons of those days; and as the Kakanfo, by the oaths of his office, must either conquer within three months or die, and Iwere is impregnable, he will have no other alternative but, as in honour bound, to make away with himself. It was arranged that he should not be forewarned but decoyed to that place until he found himself at the foot of the hill on which Iwere was built. But private intelligence had reached the Kakanfo at Ilorin of all the plots and intrigues going on in the capital. The army at length stood before Iwere, and the royal party, pointing to it, said: "This is the town to be taken by the order of the Alafin." The time was now come for the mutiny to break out: the watchword was given "O Ya!" (now is the time) and so the whole army turned their swords upon the royal party and massacred them. Chief Opele of Gbogun in particular was famous as a swordsman, and took to himself a name "A ri agada pa aburo Oba" — one who has a blade for slaying the King's brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The siege was immediately raised, and the whole army stood before the city for forty and two days. At last an empty covered calabash was sent to the King — for his head. A plain indication that he was rejected. There being no alternative, His Majesty set his house in order; but before he committed suicide, he stepped out into the palace quadrangle with face stern and resolute, carrying in his hands an earthenware dish and three arrows. He shot one to the North, one to the South, and one to the West, uttering those ever-memorable imprecations: "My curse be on ye for your disloyalty and disobedience, so let your children disobey you. If you send them on an errand, let them never return to bring you word again. To all the points I shot my arrows will ye be carried as slaves. My curse will carry you to the sea and beyond the seas; slaves will rule over you, and you their masters will become slaves."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: With this he raised and dashed the earthenware dish on the ground, smashing it into pieces, saying: "Igba la isu a ki isu awo, beheni ki oru mi o se to! to!" — a broken calabash can be mended, but not a broken dish; so let my words be — irrevocable! He then took poison and died, after which the camp was broken up, and each of the chiefs repaired to his own place. From this time the spirit of rebellion and independence began to spread throughout the kingdom: tribute was no longer paid to the King, and this was the commencement of the break-up of the unity of the Yoruba kingdom and the beginning of the tribal independence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part III ch. I (1921); not verbatim.
